original_title: NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation
article_content:
Picture moving the Cadiere grasper, grasping the gallbladder, and lifting it, all within a generated surgical scene that responds in real time. Today, we take the next step and introduce Cosmos3-H-Dreams, bringing interactive generative simulation to the visual and procedural complexity of clinical surgery with our most convincing in-body imagery to date.

Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism.

Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential.

Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment.

Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion.

Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano, a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment, and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction.

The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput.

Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams.

We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics.

Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive.  Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Se

original_title: NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability
article_content:
NVIDIA Kumo Forecast (formerly known as NV-Tesseract Forecasting) is a multi-variate time-series forecasting model that combines a pretrained Transformer backbone with Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR), a context-enhanced forecasting mode that blends direct model predictions with patterns retrieved from historical data. This includes interpretability of the results. Built on the MOMENT-1-large backbone, Kumo Forecast uses an approximately 340-million-parameter base encoder plus a trainable forecasting head.

The library provides a DataFrame-first API, configurable forecast horizons, optional historical context for retrieval, and an interpretability framework that produces horizon-specific explanations without modifying the underlying forecaster.

Kumo-Forecast is available under Apache 2.0 license.

Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS
Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast

A forecasting system can draw on two different sources of information: representations learned during pretraining and historical observations available for the current application. Kumo-Forecast brings these together through a pretrained forecasting model and an optional retrieval pathway over historical context.

In its direct forecasting path, Kumo-Forecast uses a MOMENT-based Transformer and a trained forecasting head to predict future values. In Domain Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR) mode, it also retrieves related patterns from historical data using a nearest-neighbor approach and combines that information with the direct forecast.

This creates a distinction between the model’s input window and its retrieval context. The input window supplies recent observations for the forecast; a separate historical DataFrame can supply additional context for pattern retrieval. Developers can adjust how strongly the final prediction relies on each pathway through the library’s configuration options.

Further information on DARR mode can be found in this published paper, Memory-Augmented Forecasting: Scalability and Generalization Across Temporal Domains

Kumo-Forecast combines four main components: a pretrained temporal encoder, a trainable forecasting head, historical-pattern retrieval mechanism and an interpretability framework.

Pretrained Temporal Representations: The model uses the MOMENT-1-large Transformer encoder as its backbone. The architecture keeps encoder and embedder weights frozen while training the forecasting head, separating the pretrained representation model from the task-specific prediction layer.

Direct Forecasting: The forecasting head maps the model’s representations to future values for the requested horizon. For horizons beyond the model’s native capability, there is support for autoregressive extension. This distinguishes a directly generated forecast from a longer forecast that extends predictions recursively.

Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval: DARR augments direct forecasting with k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from historical context data. This process combines direct forecasts with historical-pattern retrieval, while the SDK accepts the historical context through a separate context_df argument.

Interpretability: Kumo-Forecasting also includes a model-agnostic interpretability framework. When enabled, it produces an explanation bundle containing lag and feature attributions per forecast horizon, semantic-flow diagnostics, trajectory-stability diagnostics, and optional embedding Integrated Gradients.These outputs accompany the forecast rather than requiring a different forecasting architecture.

Further details on interpretability can be found in this paper, NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates

Data must be numeric, temporal data. Supported input sequence lengths include 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 observations. Inputs consist of a timestamp column and one or more numeric value columns, represented as a pandas DataFrame or a CSV/JSON input. W

original_title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime
original_summary: An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using...
article_content:
NVIDIA Sentry governs agent access requests, monitors runtime activity, and contains threats from an isolated hardware security layer in milliseconds.

An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them.

NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA, runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs, and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries.

Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity.

This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software.

An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host.

NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent.

Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge.

In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs, while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior.

DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy, the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment.

Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world.

An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks.
